Title: WormFinding
Loaction: Brooklyn Navy Yard, Brooklyn, NY, USA
Area: ARC 606 Architectural Design Studio III · Syracuse University School of Architecture
Project Introduction: WormFinding treats a living builder as a form-finding engine. Superworms (Zophobas morio larvae) eat extruded polystyrene and leave behind a single, connected network of galleries: they eat through the core of a foam block, keep the skin almost intact and join every gallery into one system. The project asks whether that behaviour, not its image, can become a design tool.
Design Concept: Foam blocks eaten by a superworm colony were photographed, split, sliced and scanned. Block_03 was cut into eleven 10 mm slices and both faces of every slice were scanned at 1200 dpi: twenty-two true sections through one network, rebuilt as a solid within 0.18 mm of the scans. 51% of the block was eaten, in one connected network of 446 branches and 4.2 m of galleries. Each measured property became a rule: a digital worm moves forward, keeps 92% of its direction, prefers the long axis, reuses open galleries and turns back near the skin. The rules grew from a calibrated Rhino 8 simulator into a Grasshopper component that erodes any closed volume in ten to fifteen seconds.
Project Summary: Not a copy of the shape of Block_03, but the behaviour of its worms, tuned with its real numbers and able to run on any closed volume. At the Brooklyn Navy Yard the same logic carves a building of voids around a data centre whose waste heat ties together superworm chambers that digest plastic, a ritual hall returning bodies to soil and a memorial garden in the voids. One graded structure replaces frame and skin, and erosion becomes the building's clock.

Title: LA Olympic Museum
Area: ARC 605 Architectural Design Studio II · Syracuse University School of Architecture
Project Introduction: The second project of the studio explores movement, sequence and program as the generators of a building. For an Olympic and Paralympic Museum in East Los Angeles, planned for the 2028 Games, on a triangular site shaped by the surrounding roads and next to the LA greenway path, the museum becomes a node between existing urban flows.
Design Concept: The Olympic timeline itself becomes the circulation: the galleries unfold along a continuous ramp that wraps around the building, from the ancient games to the modern Olympics. At 1:12 a ramp needs about 120 ft per floor; the constraint became the idea. Inside the wrapped core, stacked floors hold interactive sports, education and media, while a spiral stair and a vertical core offer short cuts across the timeline.
Project Summary: The ramp turns the museum inside out. Visitors moving along it are seen from the street, and the building reads as a network of paths rather than a closed box: about 37,000 sq ft of timeline galleries, interactive sports, education and media, auditorium, café and archive, held together by one slow, continuous route.

Title: LA Train Station
Area: ARC 605 Architectural Design Studio II · Syracuse University School of Architecture
Project Introduction: The first project of the studio treats a small building as a node in Los Angeles' network of flows. Ahead of the 2028 Olympics, which the city uses to accelerate its Twenty-eight by '28 transport projects, a new light-rail station and transit hub replaces the 17th Street/SMC stop on the E Line in Santa Monica, where the line meets the end of the Expo bike path.
Design Concept: The project began with a tectonic case study of Go Hasegawa's House in a Forest, rebuilt as a model and an exploded drawing to understand how one roof can define a whole space. Abstract projective models then tested folding, spanning and enclosure as operations, translating the case study into a language for the station.
Project Summary: A single folded roof of triangulated, translucent panels gathers the station under one shaded canopy and gives it an identity along the line. Beneath it, freestanding volumes for ticketing, security and administration, a café, a climate-controlled waiting room and restrooms sit along one open circulation spine; the roof is built in layers, from cladding and outer space frame to primary structure, sub-structures and ground.

Title: Saleria
Area: ARC 604 Architectural Design Studio I · Syracuse University School of Architecture
Project Introduction: Saleria is an experiment in aggregation architecture: structures of many loose, identical elements held together by friction and geometry rather than permanent joints. The name joins the Italian “sale” and “-eria”: “the place of salt.” It continues my earlier project ESTA, where star-thistle-inspired interlocking modules were first tested as a self-supporting bridge.
Design Concept: Tests compared stars, tripods, tetrapods and flat modules. A 14-spike star close to the purple starthistle interlocked best, forming columns, arches and porous envelopes: longer arms add reach but lower density, sharper spikes improve grip, and higher density adds strength at the cost of material. Hundreds of 3D-printed modules pushed the system toward stars about three metres across. Many aggregates failed until sand became temporary formwork: stars draped over sand mounds held as arches and semi-domes once it was removed.
Project Summary: On the site beside the Everson Museum the sand berms are laid out first and the stars are aggregated over them; sand becomes the foundation too, and salt crystallization binds the surface. Inspired by Iran's salt caves, Yanhu Lake and Michael Heizer's earthworks, Saleria is a luminous, reversible architecture where structure emerges from aggregation rather than construction.

Title: Shelter
Loaction: Chittenango, NY, USA · Empire State Trail
Area: ARC 604 Architectural Design Studio I · Syracuse University School of Architecture
Project Introduction: The second project of the studio continued the study of movement and transformation and introduced scale and occupation. It began with the body: the human form was scanned and modelled to read its scales and the surfaces and spaces it produces as it moves through space and time.
Design Concept: “All movement is the product of two factors: time and space; to know the movement of a body is to know the series of positions which it occupies in space during a series of successive instants.” (Étienne-Jules Marey, 1868). The shelter reuses the faceted logic of the salt vessel: a folded shell of planes that wraps around two bodies.
Project Summary: A free-standing shelter on the Empire State Trail, beside the preserved Erie Canal in Chittenango, for two people who may or may not know one another. A reinvention of the primitive hut, it opens to the canal and answers wind, light and weather: an architecture of fragility and change rather than of control over nature.

Title: Performative Vessels
Area: ARC 604 Architectural Design Studio I · Syracuse University School of Architecture
Project Introduction: Architecture is usually imagined as permanent and stable; this vessel begins in instability. Laid on its side, it becomes upright only as it is filled with salt.
Design Concept: Made of translucent and transparent acrylic, the vessel does not conceal: salt penetrates its perforations and reveals the inside, and light amplifies its behaviour. It echoes the Persian proverb: “From the vessel flows only what it contains.”
Project Summary: Salt is expressive, not silent. The vessel demonstrates its content, tipping upright as it fills: a first study of behaviour and transformation that the studio carried into the shelter and Saleria.

Title: Endemic Architecture
Area: ARC 681 Media I · Syracuse University School of Architecture
Project Introduction: Media I treated drawing and modelling as tools of analysis. Part 3C studied the work of Bolles + Wilson and their idea of an endemic architecture: buildings that grow out of the particular conditions of their place.
Design Concept: The reading was translated into line studies and sections, and the lines were folded into paper models, each fold recording a change in the drawing.
Project Summary: The studies end in a cast model: the folded paper becomes a mould, and the drawing becomes a surface of light and shadow.

Title: Porta Verde
Area: Architectural Design Studio + Sustainable Building Technologies Studio · Politecnico di Milano
Services: Prof. Filippo Paolo Pagliani, Prof. Gabriele Masera, Prof. Matteo Brasca
Team: Seyed Mojtaba Mohammadi, Raha Alaei, Yared Bekele, Sima Delkhosh, Amr Elkhouly, Ali Elsayed, Hanieh Farhad, Mobina Honarvar, Beantenew Lemma, Ali Navabi, Padideh Poormehrabi
Project Introduction: This project joins two complementary studios, Architectural Design and Sustainable Building Technologies, into one proposal: a building in Milan that works as productive and social urban infrastructure while advancing sustainability, adaptability and ecological integration. At its core, nature, work and public life coexist.
Design Concept: Over ten massing options, from courtyard to atrium types, were compared by surface-to-volume ratio and estimated energy use; option 9 was chosen for its architectural value. Daylight simulations and climate studies set the orientation, depletions and façade structure. Step by step the energy use intensity fell from 284 kWh/m² for a standard office to about 68 kWh/m², with 76% of occupied hours within 18–27 °C; PV panels produce about 300,000 kWh a year, 87% of the building's need. A ground-source heat pump and a solar chimney drive natural stack ventilation, and glulam, CLT and LVL form the timber structure, checked in Altair S-TIMBER.
Project Summary: Integration rather than addition runs through the project: rooftop gardens and vertical farming shape its identity, social programs interlock with the courtyard landscape, and daylight, shading, ventilation and energy set the spatial hierarchy. 4,639 m² of café, market, vertical farming, co-working, workshops and restaurant become one self-regulating building.

Title: Harvesting the Future
Area: Urban Design + Building Renovation Studio · M.Sc. Building and Architectural Engineering · Politecnico di Milano
Services: Prof. Angela Colucci, Prof. Sara Lodrini, Prof. Manuela Grecchi
Team: Asma Aboudief, Chiara Berti, Ali Elsayed, Hanieh Farhad, Tanay Mahajan, Seyed Mojtaba Mohammadi, Padideh Poormehrabi, Amr Tarek
Project Introduction: San Cristoforo lies on the south-western edge of Milan, where the Naviglio Grande, the railway and the new M4 metro line meet. Once an agricultural belt of canals and rice fields, the area is now cut apart by infrastructure, and Aldo Rossi's former terminal building stands unfinished beside the canal.
Design Concept: The concept follows four steps: connect, with walkways and cycle paths that stitch San Cristoforo into the urban fabric; renature, with green corridors and ponds that follow the topography; a spine, a horizontal main axis that orders the functions from public to private; and entrances, promenades and bridges over the canal and the railway. Seventy per cent of the site becomes an ecological park of orchards, community gardens, a wetland and botanical gardens; thirty per cent holds the public functions.
Project Summary: The renovation of Rossi's terminal keeps its volume and structure and works with reversible interventions: an incremental, modular approach turns it into affordable housing, from studios and family flats to duplexes and lofts that can grow over time, around a community centre. A green roof, arched skylights, movable louvres and light, interchangeable materials make it the heart of the Green Oasis.

Title: Sustainable Multidisciplinary Design
Area: SMDP Studio · Sustainable Multidisciplinary Design Process · Politecnico di Milano
Team: Göksu Aktün, Chiara Berti, Ali Elsayed, Hanieh Farhad, Seyed Mojtaba Mohammadi
Project Introduction: Set on a Reinventing Cities site at Nodo Bovisa in Milan, the studio asked for mixed urban functions in harmony with the context, a better station and public space, and improved interchange services.
Design Concept: Using the IMM methodology for complex adaptive systems, the site was read horizontally and vertically to find its weak links: few types of use and poor connections between its western and eastern parts. The area was divided into three parts, the volumes were excavated into courtyards and separated along a central axis, and a solar study set their heights.
Project Summary: The answer is a new, walkable urban centre and gateway to Milan, built on social housing, production and social engagement, with denser blocks within a five-minute walk of the station. Two bridges join east and west, one for tram 2 and one for walking and cycling, and a residential tower in timber and concrete stands at its heart.

Title: Topo Bridge
Area: Bionic Architectural Technology Master's Thesis · Pars University of Architecture and Art
Services: Dr. Mohammadreza Matini (supervisor), Dr. Morteza Rahbar (advisor)
Project Introduction: Engineers, designers and architects have always been inspired by nature. Biological phenomena are the best engineering examples: what remains today are the forms that survived natural selection. An organism's development and the evolution of its structure over generations is called morphogenesis, and topology optimization makes it possible to simulate it and apply it to structures in which form and structure are one.
Design Concept: The bridge links Chitgar Lake, a growing tourist attraction, with Chitgar Forest Park, a place for gathering and recreation, over 254 m. Initial lines and volumes were drawn from the existing paths; the volume was split into segments, each given its loads and supports, and the solver placed material only where it was needed. The optimized segments were assembled into one structure, and the decks were designed by tracking the forces.
Project Summary: The result is remarkably close to organic forms. The decks carry separate tracks for cyclists, runners and pedestrians, with places to gather and planted areas along the way, and open where the structure divides; two entrances reach the bridge from the north and four from the south.

Title: ESTA
Area: Architectural Bionic Technology Design Studio 03 · Pars University of Architecture and Art
Project Introduction: ESTA is an aggregated bridge: a large arrangement of loose elements, continuously observed and modulated by the architect at the particle or system level, that together perform the architectural and structural tasks of a bridge. The name is of Italian origin and means “from the east”; in Spanish it also means “this”: simple, pure and bare-bones.
Design Concept: Observations and experiments showed the sharp yellow thistle of Centaurea calcitrapa, the purple star thistle common in the Middle East, to be the best natural particle for interlocking into arcs. The aggregate element has 14 spikes, seven in each of two planes. After physical tests, the aggregation was simulated in 3ds Max MassFX; chained modules were tested at the lower levels, and two buttresses inspired by honey locust thorns anchor the bridge on both banks.
Project Summary: Decks sit on the last aggregated levels and serve specific architectural functions: a breathing space and viewpoint, a place for food and drink around the elevators, and a gallery of light and shadow where daylight filters through the modules. ESTA is the beginning of the aggregation research that Saleria later continued and completed.

Title: Digitalized Versatile Mold
Area: Digital Architectural Technology Project · Advanced Application of Computer in Architecture · Pars University of Architecture and Art
Team: Group of five students, with Seyed Mojtaba Mohammadi
Project Introduction: Developed with four other students in a digital technology course, the project is a digitally driven, versatile mold for heterogeneous facade bricks: one mold on the production line casts a whole family of bricks, so a facade can vary unit by unit.
Design Concept: An acrylic frame holds four actuated elements around a central diaphragm; the algorithm moves them to a new position for every brick before the concrete is poured.
Project Summary: One mold, many bricks: the same device produced a family of openings that vary in angle, depth and shape across the facade. Linked to an Arduino board, it could turn the facade into a responsive skin adjusting light, pattern or enclosure.

Title: Active Bending Gridshell
Area: Workshop · Bending-Active Gridshells · Faculty of Architecture, University of Tehran
Project Introduction: An active-bending gridshell is a doubly curved lattice built from long, initially straight and flexible members that are bent elastically into shape. The bending stresses stored in the members, the connections of the grid and its double curvature together give the structure its stiffness: form, structure and assembly are found together instead of being imposed.
Design Concept: Light, quick to erect and economical in material, gridshells can span large areas with very little matter, from Frei Otto's Mannheim Multihalle (1975) to the Weald and Downland and Savill gridshells in England. The team studied these precedents and form-found a triangulated gridshell digitally.
Project Summary: In a three-day workshop at the Faculty of Architecture of the University of Tehran, the gridshell was cut, assembled and raised at full scale.
